source.title: Consistency-Aware Editing for Entity-level Unlearning in Language Models
source.authors: Xiaoqi Han; V'ictor Guti'errez-Basulto; Ru Li; Xiao-Li Li; Ji-Ye Liang; Jeff Z. Pan

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether unlearning suppresses entity knowledge across varied and adversarial prompt forms, a conceptual test of prompt-based recovery rather than the claimed fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, or quantization attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates CAE and comparator unlearning methods using varied forget-set prompts, including in-context learning, prefix injection, role play, synonym manipulation, and cross-lingual queries. The causal-tracing analysis measures where entity knowledge influences outputs, but does not test whether ablating a direction after unlearning restores knowledge. It reports no post-unlearning relearning-set fine-tuning or quantization attack.
record.test_reason: A new editing-based unlearning method (CAE) is evaluated on RWKU's adversarial prompt probes (prefix injection, role play, in-context, cross-lingual and others) after unlearning. Its results therefore bear on whether prompting recovers forgotten entity knowledge (E), whether the method resists such attacks (F), and whether unlearning lowers forget accuracy while keeping utility (A). There are no fine-tuning, direction-ablation or quantization attacks. The causal tracing is done before unlearning, so it does not bear on C.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CAE, a consistency-regularized low-rank MLP edit, beats prior unlearning and editing baselines on RWKU and ToFU in forgetting and efficiency, with a better forget–retain trade-off and leakage resistance across paraphrases. They note it is weaker when the entity name is implicit, such as synonym manipulation, and that batch and sequential extension remains open.
record.recipe_differences: CAE is consistency-aware, low-rank MLP editing using selected entity-related prompts and aligned residuals; it is not the gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, or RMU recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt type changes the reported forgetting score; the authors specifically identify implicit entity references such as synonym manipulation as harder. Editing last subject token versus last token also changes CAE performance, but this is not a recovery attack.
record.problems: No chance-level comparison is reported for the forget scores. The paper evaluates one family of prompt-based probes but not post-unlearning fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization. Results are reported as averages across unlearning instances; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted other Table IV comparator results except selected EMMET and MEMIT synonym and cross-lingual rows (r23-r30); the remaining comparator cells are not needed to show CAE's prompt results or the variation in comparator outcomes. Other metrics and method comparisons unrelated to forgotten-knowledge recovery were also omitted.

untested.parts: No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No direction ablation after unlearning. Causal tracing is done only on base models to localize knowledge; there is no block-vs-delete analysis of the edited model.
CAE's resistance to fine-tuning, ablation and quantization attacks is not tested; only prompt probes are.
Chance level for the forget metrics is not stated, so 'near chance' cannot be checked.

missing.what: Aggregate forget (FB/QA/AA/All), neighbor, MIA and utility for CAE and all baselines; needed for A's 'keeps general ability' part. CAE All goes 79.6→15.9 and AA 77.7→22.0 on Llama3.
Simple-question and other cells for AlphaEdit, EMMET and MEMIT, needed as within-method baselines for E. AlphaEdit barely forgets (e.g. 0.566 SQ vs 0.718 before).
10-subject comparison including latent-adversarial GA/NPO and CAE AA scores.
Qwen2.5-7B CAE forget results: AA 55.5→24.5, QA 44.7→12.6.
Qualitative paraphrase leakage: MEMIT, EMMET and AlphaEdit output Jackie Chan facts while CAE does not.

record.verdict_notes: The record used before-unlearning values as the baseline for every Table IV row. For E (does prompting recover knowledge), the right reference is each method's own post-unlearning simple-question score, so states were re-graded on that basis. Row states for r1-r22 refer to E recovery; for F, an absent state means CAE resisted. The comparator rows are editing methods, not the new method, so F was removed from them. The record's F limits_scope label with no rows was dropped; those parts are listed as untested. Multiple-choice scores may be inflated by guessing, since chance level is not stated. This is a method paper, not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not state a chance level for the reported forget scores, and does not establish that the tested methods reach near-chance performance.
No attack fine-tunes an unlearned model on a small set of unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten facts.
No post-unlearning activation-direction ablation is tested, and the paper does not establish that CAE blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No quantization of unlearned weights is tested.
Tests several prompt styles and cross-lingual probes, but does not report jailbreaks or recovery using in-context information as a separate attack beyond the listed RWKU prompt categories.
CAE is evaluated on varied prompt types, but the paper does not test resistance to post-unlearning fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization.
